## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: What Google Search Console's New Platform Properties Mean for Your Social and Video Content

Google Search Console now lets you create a dedicated property for your Instagram, TikTok, X or YouTube account — separate from your website — and see which search terms sent people to that content on Google Search and Discover. This feature, called platform properties, launched on 7 July 2026, and it changes a genuine blind spot: until now, a digital marketing agency in Pune reporting on your website's SEO had no official way to show that your Instagram Reel or YouTube video was also showing up in Google's own search results, because Search Console only ever measured your website.

If your brand invests real budget in Instagram Reels, YouTube videos, or short-form content on TikTok or X, and your monthly marketing report has never once mentioned how that content performs in Google Search itself — not the platform's own native analytics, but Google Search — that's the gap this article is about closing.

## What a Platform Property Actually Is

A platform property is a new property type inside Search Console, alongside the domain and URL-prefix properties most businesses already have for their website. Instead of verifying ownership of a website, you connect and authorise a social or video account directly: Instagram, TikTok, X, or YouTube are the four supported platforms at launch. Once connected, Search Console starts showing you which search queries on Google led people to that specific account's content, and how that content performed in Google's results.

This matters because posts on these platforms are frequently indexable and can rank in Google Search and Discover on their own, independent of whether you also have a website. A boutique that only sells through Instagram and has no traditional website can now still see, in an official Google product, exactly which searches are driving people to their posts — something that was previously invisible unless you were guessing from the platform's own in-app insights, which don't show Google Search behaviour at all.

### Setting one up

The process mirrors verifying a normal Search Console property, with one difference: instead of proving you own a domain, you authorise the connection from inside your Instagram, TikTok, X or YouTube account. In Search Console, you go to the property selector, choose "Add property," select the platform, and follow the authorisation flow, which typically requires you to be logged into the account you're connecting with the right admin permissions. Once verified, data starts appearing in three places: the Performance report (queries, impressions, clicks, position — the same structure as a normal website property), the Insights report, and Achievements, a newer Search Console section that surfaces specific wins Google thinks are worth flagging.

Google has said the rollout is gradual, so if you don't see the option to add a platform property immediately, that's expected rather than a sign something's broken on your end — check back over the following weeks rather than assuming the feature isn't reaching your account.

## Why This Is a Genuinely New Reporting Category, Not a Rebrand of Something Old

It's worth being precise about what this is not. It is not the same as the AI Overviews and AI Mode reporting Search Console added earlier in 2026 for website properties, which shows how your existing web pages perform inside Google's generative search surfaces. Platform properties are about a different content type entirely — your social and video accounts, which may have no associated website at all, or where the website and the social account perform completely differently in search and deserve to be reported on separately rather than lumped into one number.

It's also not the same as the analytics you already get from Instagram, TikTok, YouTube or X themselves. Those platforms tell you what happened on their own platform — views, saves, shares, watch time, native search inside the app. None of them tell you whether someone searched for something on Google itself and landed on your Reel or video as a result. That's specifically what Search Console's platform properties add: visibility into Google's own search behaviour around your social content, which is a genuinely different signal from in-app engagement metrics.

## What This Changes for a Digital Marketing Agency in Pune

If your agency runs both your social content and your SEO, this closes a reporting gap that made those two disciplines look artificially disconnected. A campaign that drove strong Instagram engagement but showed nothing in your website's SEO numbers used to look, on paper, like it had zero organic search impact. Platform properties can now show whether that same content was actually being found through Google Search, even though the destination was Instagram rather than your website — evidence that the work was contributing to search visibility all along, just not in the place your reporting used to look.

Practically, this should change three things in how a competent agency reports on your account from here:

### 1. Social content stops being reported only on vanity metrics

Likes, comments and shares from the platform's native analytics are still useful, but they answer "did people on the platform like this," not "did this show up when someone searched for something related to my business on Google." Platform property data answers the second question, and for a business trying to understand its actual discoverability, that's frequently the more useful number.

### 2. Query-level insight into what's actually working

Just like the website Performance report, platform properties show the specific search terms bringing people to your content. If your Instagram account is repeatedly surfacing for a particular product or service query, that's a strong, specific signal about what content to make more of — far more actionable than "this post did better than that post" from in-app insights alone.

### 3. It surfaces content you might not think of as "SEO work"

A short video answering a common customer question, posted natively to Instagram or YouTube with no link back to your website, has historically fallen outside anything an SEO report measured. Platform properties bring that content inside the same measurement framework as your website's organic search performance, which is a meaningful shift in what "SEO" even covers for a business that publishes across multiple platforms.

## How This Interacts With the New Branded Queries Filter

Search Console separately expanded its branded queries filter to all eligible properties in 2026 — a feature that automatically splits your Performance report data into "branded" queries (your brand name, close misspellings, and brand-associated product or service terms) versus "non-branded" queries (everything else), applied automatically by Google's own classification rather than a list you define yourself. It's available as a filter option on the query dimension in the Performance report, alongside the existing keyword filter, and it applies across search types — web, image, video and news.

The two features are worth using together rather than separately. A website property showing mostly branded-query traffic tells a very different story than one earning meaningful non-branded impressions — the first means people already knew you and searched your name; the second means Google is surfacing you to people who didn't know you existed yet, which is the harder, more valuable win. Applying the same branded/non-branded lens to a platform property, once it's available there, tells you whether your Instagram or YouTube content is reaching new audiences through search or mostly being found by people who were already following you and searched your name directly. If your agency's monthly report currently reports one blended organic number with no branded/non-branded split, that's now a data quality gap worth fixing, and it costs nothing beyond turning on a filter that already exists in your account.

## A Practical Setup Checklist

Setting up a platform property is straightforward, but a few things are worth confirming before you hand it to whoever manages your social accounts.

- **Confirm who has admin access.** Verifying a platform property requires authorising the connection from inside the actual Instagram, TikTok, X or YouTube account, so whoever does this needs genuine admin-level access, not just posting access. If your agency manages the account on your behalf, confirm they have the right level of access rather than discovering mid-setup that they don't.
- **Set one up per platform you actively use for discovery**, not every account your business happens to have. A dormant X account that hasn't posted in a year won't generate meaningful data, and adding it mainly adds noise to what your team has to check monthly.
- **Give it time before judging the data.** Because the feature rolled out gradually through the second half of 2026, and because Google needs time to associate search activity with a newly connected account, don't expect a complete picture in the first few days. Treat the first month as a baseline-gathering period rather than a verdict on whether the content is "working."
- **Decide who actually reviews the Insights and Achievements sections.** These are newer parts of Search Console that surface specific, Google-flagged observations rather than raw numbers, and they're easy to ignore if nobody owns checking them. Assign it to whoever already owns your monthly SEO or social reporting rather than leaving it to no one.
- **Cross-reference with your website property**, if you have one. If a product or service query shows strong impressions on your website property but weak or no equivalent activity on a platform property for the same topic, or vice versa, that's a genuine content gap worth investigating rather than a coincidence.

## What Early Data Typically Looks Like

Businesses that have started using platform properties since the July 2026 launch report a pattern worth expecting rather than being surprised by: impressions in Google Search for social content tend to be concentrated around a smaller set of posts than you'd guess from in-app engagement alone. A Reel that performed only moderately on Instagram's own metrics can show up disproportionately in Google Search data if it happens to answer a specific, searchable question — "how to," "cost of," "best," and comparison-style phrasing tend to travel well into Google's index regardless of how a post performed natively. Conversely, posts that did very well on-platform in likes and shares sometimes show close to zero Google Search impressions, because they weren't phrased or framed around anything a person would type into a search box.

This is useful precisely because it doesn't match in-app performance. If your content strategy has been optimised purely for platform engagement — hooks, trends, watch-time retention — platform property data gives you a second, independent signal about which of that same content is also earning you free discovery through Google Search, which is a different and often more durable source of traffic than an algorithm-dependent feed.

## What To Actually Ask Your Agency This Month

If you work with a digital marketing agency in Pune and want to know whether they're keeping up with this change, these are direct, checkable questions:

- Have you set up a platform property for our Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or X account, or explained why it isn't a priority for us specifically?
- Can you show me which search queries are actually driving discovery of our social content, separate from in-app engagement metrics?
- Is our monthly report split between branded and non-branded query performance, or is it one blended organic number?
- If we don't have a website — or our website and social presence tell very different stories — how is that being reported now that the tools exist to separate them?

An agency actively using these features will have specific numbers to show you. One that hasn't heard of platform properties yet — a feature that's been live since July 2026 — is working from a reporting toolkit that's already a few months behind what Google itself now offers for free.

## A Realistic Caveat

Not every business needs to rush to set this up. If your social accounts exist mainly for brand presence and customer service rather than as a discovery channel, and your website already carries the bulk of your organic search traffic, platform properties are a nice-to-have rather than an urgent fix. Where it matters most is for businesses whose product discovery genuinely happens on Instagram, YouTube or similar platforms — fashion, food, home decor, fitness, and services that lean heavily on short-form video and visual content — where a meaningful share of "SEO" in the older sense is now happening outside the website entirely, in the sense that no rankings tool built for websites was ever built to see.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I need a website to use Search Console's platform properties?

No. Platform properties verify ownership of a social or video account directly, not a website. A business or creator with only an Instagram or YouTube presence and no traditional website can still set one up and see how that content performs in Google Search and Discover.

### Which platforms are supported by Search Console's platform properties?

At launch on 7 July 2026, Instagram, TikTok, X and YouTube are supported. Google has described the rollout as gradual, so availability and any additional platforms may expand over time.

### Is platform property data the same as my Instagram or YouTube analytics?

No. The platform's own analytics show engagement that happened on that platform — views, likes, saves, watch time. Search Console's platform property shows something different: which Google Search queries led people to that content, and how it performed specifically in Google's search results and Discover feed.

### What's the difference between platform properties and the branded queries filter?

They're separate features that work well together. Platform properties add a new data source — your social and video content's search performance. The branded queries filter, available on both website and (as it rolls out) platform properties, splits any Performance report into branded versus non-branded query traffic, showing whether people found you by name or found you without knowing you existed yet.

### How long does it take for platform property data to start showing after setup?

Search Console has not published a fixed timeline, and as with website properties, data typically populates over the following days as Google processes search activity related to the connected account. Because the rollout itself is gradual, some accounts may see the option to add a platform property later than others.

## Where to Start

If your Instagram, YouTube or other social content plays any real role in how customers find you, setting up a platform property costs nothing and takes a few minutes once the option appears in your account. The value is in what it tells you afterward — genuine search-query data about content that used to be a measurement blind spot.
